catalog_citation: Jakobi, Angelika & Ahmed Hamdan. 2015. Number Marking on Karko Nouns. Dotawo: A Journal of Nubian Studies 2: 271-289. doi:10.5070/D62110017 (eScholarship open access, CC BY-NC)
catalog_locator: sec. 2 'Phonology, syllable structure, and morphophonemic alternations', p. 274 and p. 276; sec. 7 'Conclusions', p. 288.
catalog_quote: Note: In order to provide space for the tonal accents, long vowels are written as double vowels in the examples below, for example, jīīl instead of jīːl, and tɛ́ɛ̀ instead of tɛ̂ː. [...] Although these examples appear to suggest that tone is “copied” to the suffix vowel, this is not the case. In fact, tone is not conceived to be a property of a vowel but rather a property of a syllable. Evidence for this is provided by lost syllables whose tones often attach to the previous syllable (for more details, see below). [p. 274] ... Falling and rising tones often reflect the loss of a syllabic suffix. The tone of that suffix is preserved by attaching to the preceding tone of the root. [p. 276] ... The function of tone in number marking on nouns has not been investigated in detail. However, our data show that certain tone patterns re-occur and that singular and plural forms can even be solely marked by tonal contrast. So the relevance of tone in number marking is apparent, but it still requires a more refined study in the context of a general investigation on tone in Karko grammar. [p. 288]
world_status: statement found in an open source

Evidence for this is provided by lost syllables whose tones often attach to the previous syllable (for more details, see below).' -- the compiler quote drops only the parenthesis). p.276 (lines 294-299) adds 'Falling and risi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Karko is analysed as a tone language (high, mid, low; falling and rising contours arising from lost syllables), with tone a property of the syllable and able to mark number on its own; the modern description says nothing about word stress. The only Karko-specific stress remark is Meinhof 1918/19 (ZfK 9: 49-50), who found the stress accent impossible to pin down ('scheinbar willkuerliche Behandlung') and had the impression of musical tones that shift with position in the sentence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Karko proper. For the Tabaq variety (Hellwig & Schneider-Blum 2014: 68, 72, 74, 76) suffix and word-final syllables are called 'unstressed' (site of vowel centralization and shortening) without a stated placement rule; Tabaq has two level tones H/L plus HL/LH contours (p. 77). Meinhof 1918/19: 49-50 (Garko): 'Die Beobachtung des Staerkeakzents ist ausserordentlich erschwert durch die scheinbar willkuerliche Behandlung desselben.. Ich habe den Eindruck, als wenn zwar musikalische Toene vorliegen, als ob sie aber durch die Stellung im Satz sich aendern' [Observation of the stress accent is made extraordinarily difficult by its apparently arbitrary treatment.. I have the impression that musical tones are indeed present, but that they change with position in the sentence].
new_statements.domain_note: Jakobi & Hamdan's tone marking is on citation forms of nouns (sg/pl pairs); no word- vs phrase-level prominence discussion. Meinhof's remark concerns elicited words and short sentences.
new_statements.identity_note: Jakobi & Hamdan 2015 describe Karko proper (kàâŋg / káákmbɛ̀ɛ̀), co-authored by a native speaker. Meinhof 1918/19 'Garko' = Karko (informants from Jebel Garko near Dulman, recorded in El-Obeid 1914). Hellwig & Schneider-Blum 2014 and Ismail 2015 describe Tabaq (t̪àànɪ̀), and Alshareef 2015 describes Abu Jinuk; Glottolog 5.1 files all of these under kark1256 (no separate glottocodes; DoReCo labels the Tabaq corpus 'Tabaq (Karko)'), whereas Ethnologue/Wikipedia note Tabaq and Abu Jinuk 'may be dialects or separate languages'. The Tabaq tone facts (2 tones) should not be transferred to Karko proper (written with H/M/L).

new_statements.quote: p.77: "Hierzu kommt, daß der dynamische Akzent im Nubischen außerordentlich schwankt. Man kann dasselbe Wort in dreifach verschiedener Betonung unmittelbar hinter einander hören.¹) [...] Herr Klingenheben erklärte in halb scherzhaftem Unmut nach langer Beschäftigung mit der Sache: „Das Nubische hat den dynamischen Akzent, aber es ist gleichgültig, auf welche Silbe man ihn legt.“ [...] ¹) So z. B. im Dialekt von Garko: budúle̱, budulé̱, búdule̱ „Hase“." p.81: "Das Vorhandensein von musikalischen Tönen im Kordofannubischen kann nicht bestritten werden. [...] für die Dialekte der Berge Garko, Gulfan, Kodro, Dulman, Dilling"
new_statements.translation: p.77: "Added to this is that the dynamic (stress) accent in Nubian fluctuates extraordinarily. One can hear the same word with three different accentuations in immediate succession.¹ [...] Mr Klingenheben declared, in half-joking exasperation after long occupation with the matter: 'Nubian has the dynamic accent, but it is immaterial on which syllable one puts it.' [...] ¹ Thus e.g. in the dialect of Garko: budúle̱, budulé̱, búdule̱ 'hare'." p.81: "The presence of musical tones in Kordofan Nubian cannot be disputed [... a finding I made] for the dialects of the hills Garko, Gulfan, Kodro, Dulman, Dilling."
new_statements.citation: Meinhof, Carl. 1916. Eine Studienfahrt nach Kordofan. Hamburg: Friederichsen, p. 77.
new_statements.locator: ch. 10 'Die nubische Sprache', p. 77 with fn. 1 (SUB Hamburg PPN1008953415 scan 0119); p. 78 fn. 2 (scan 0120); p. 81 (scan 0123). 77), 717-779 (p.78), 909-972 (p.81).
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (scan 0119 block, lines ~657-716) and the page scan cropped and viewed). p.77 main text is there word for word: 'Hierzu kommt, dass der dynamische Akzent im Nubischen ausserordentlich schwankt. Man kann dasselbe Wort in dreifach verschiedener Betonung unmittelbar hinter einander hoeren.1) Ausserdem koennen gerade hier dialektische Unterschiede vorliegen.. Herr Klingenheben erklaerte in halb scherzhaftem Unmut nach langer Beschaeftigung mit der Sache: "Das Nubische hat den dynamischen Akzent, aber es ist gleichgueltig, auf welche Silbe man ihn legt." Wenn ich ihn recht verstand, meinte er, dass der Starkton im Nubischen "schwebend" ist wie im Franzoesischen, nicht feststehend wie im D…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's tone-language reading (Jakobi & Hamdan 2015: H/M/L tones, no stress statement) and with the already-held Meinhof 1918/19 ZfK Garko excerpt ('Die Beobachtung des Stärkeakzents ist außerordentlich erschwert durch die scheinbar willkürliche Behandlung desselben'); adds the explicit observation, with a Garko example, that stress placement varies freely over the syllables of a word (no fixed stress position) and the explicit claim that Garko has musical tones. Confirms the first-pass conjecture about what p. 77 says. No placement rule is given, so nothing contradicts the catalog (whose rule field is empty).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Meinhof reports that dynamic (stress) accent in Nubian is highly unstable: the same word can be heard with stress on any of its three syllables in succession, his example being Garko (= Karko) budúle̱ / budulé̱ / búdule̱ 'hare'; he relays Klingenheben's classification that Nubian has stress but it does not matter which syllable carries it ('schwebend' like French, not fixed like German, English, Arabic). Separately he states that Kordofan Nubian, Garko included, definitely has musical (lexical) tones (p. 81; p. 78 fn. 2: Heinitz found sure musical tones in Kordofan Nubian from the phonograms, only rudiments in Nile Nubian). I.e. tone present, word stress not fixed to any syllable and not reliably determinable.
new_statements.exceptions: He allows that dialect differences may underlie conflicting stress reports (p. 77: 'Außerdem können gerade hier dialektische Unterschiede vorliegen'); Klingenheben's characterisation of the stress as 'schwebend' (hovering) as in French; p. 78: Nile Nubian speakers do not pronounce a given word consistently with high/mid/low tone 'wie das sonst im Sudanischen geschieht', whereas Kordofan Nubian has sure musical tones (fn. 2, printed with the typo 'musikaclishe [sic] Töne'). Much of the main-text discussion on p. 76-78 concerns 'das Nubische' in general and the Nile Nubian grammars of Reinisch and Lepsius; the Garko footnote and p. 81 are the Kordofan-specific statements.
new_statements.identity_note: Meinhof's 'Garko' is Karko (Glottolog lists Garko as an alternative name for kark1256); his p. 77 main text generalises over 'das Nubische' (largely the Nile Nubian described by Reinisch and Lepsius), with the Garko forms given in footnote 1 as the concrete example and Garko named on p. 81 among the Kordofan hill dialects (Garko, Gulfan, Kodro, Dulman, Dilling) he recorded in El-Obeid in 1914. The copy read is the SUB Hamburg digitization (PPN1008953415) of the same 1916 Friederichsen edition as the HathiTrust Cornell copy named in open_url.

tone.says: For Karko (not Wali): data are transcribed with high, mid, low, falling and rising tone marks; the authors state that tone is a property of the syllable (tones of lost syllables re-attach to the preceding syllable, yielding contours), that tonal alternations accompany number marking and that singular/plural can be distinguished by tone alone; a full study of Karko tone is deferred to Jakobi's unpublished Kordofan Nubian monograph (fn 1). No tone inventory count is stated.
